SRC-001.prerequisites: Read access to the application's source code, specifically the CORS/middleware configuration files. A running build of the application (local or a test environment) and an HTTP client (curl/Burp Suite) to confirm the configuration's runtime behavior matches what the code implies.
SRC-001.whatItIs: Looking directly at the code, the setting that controls which websites are allowed to make cross-origin requests is too permissive — it either automatically trusts whatever website is asking, allows literally any website plus lets them send credentials, or checks the requesting site's name in a loose way (like just checking it contains the right word) instead of matching against an exact, specific list of allowed sites.
SRC-001.rootCause: This setting was written to quickly satisfy an immediate need — letting one or more frontends talk to the API — using the simplest possible approach (trust anything, or match loosely) instead of maintaining an exact, specific list of the actual sites that should be trusted.
SRC-001.impact: A malicious web page loaded in a victim's browser can make authenticated cross-origin requests to the API using the victim's existing session/cookies and read the response, exfiltrating data or performing state-changing actions the victim's session is authorized for — the exact severity depends on whether credentialed requests are also permitted alongside the permissive origin match.
stepsToIdentify: Locate the CORS configuration/middleware in source (searching for `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, a CORS middleware package's configuration block, or a custom origin-matching function).
Read the origin-matching logic precisely: does it echo the request's Origin header unconditionally, use a wildcard, or apply a substring/suffix match rather than an exact-match allowlist.

Check whether `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is also configured alongside the permissive origin match, which is the combination that makes the misconfiguration exploitable for credentialed requests.

Build and run the application locally with the identified configuration, then confirm the runtime behavior matches the source by sending a request with an arbitrary `Origin` header and inspecting the response.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes CORS-misconfiguration testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Send a test request with an arbitrary `Origin` header and confirm the response reflects it back (or otherwise matches the permissive pattern identified in source).
Build a benign proof-of-concept HTML page issuing a credentialed cross-origin request to the application from a different test origin.
Load the proof-of-concept page in a browser session authenticated to the application (a test account) and confirm the cross-origin response is successfully read.
Document the exact source location of the misconfigured origin-matching logic and the confirmed runtime exploitability.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

SRC-002.prerequisites: Read access to the application's file-upload-handling source code. A running build of the application and an HTTP client (curl/Burp Suite) to test the identified logic's runtime behavior.
SRC-002.whatItIs: Looking at the upload code directly: it decides what kind of file was uploaded — and how to handle it — based purely on what the client claims the file type is (through a header or the filename's extension), instead of actually inspecting the file's real content. An attacker can label a malicious file with an innocent-looking type and have it accepted.
SRC-002.rootCause: The claimed file type and filename extension are both values the client fully controls and can set to anything. Trusting either one for a security decision — like whether it's safe to store somewhere web-accessible — mixes up 'what the client says this is' with 'what it actually is,' and an attacker can easily make those two things different.
SRC-002.impact: An attacker can upload a file whose actual content is executable/dangerous (a web shell, an HTML file with embedded script) while its declared `Content-Type`/extension claims it's an innocuous type (an image), potentially resulting in stored XSS if the file is later served with its attacker-controlled type, or direct code execution if the file lands somewhere the web server will execute it.
stepsToIdentify: Locate the file-upload handling code and trace exactly what determines the file's accepted/rejected status and its stored/served type — the client-supplied `Content-Type` header, the filename's extension, or an independent content inspection.
Confirm whether any magic-byte/signature-based content verification exists at all, distinct from a client-supplied metadata check.

Build and run the application, then attempt to upload a file with mismatched content and declared type (e.g. an HTML file with a script payload, declared as `image/png` with a `.png` extension) and observe whether it's accepted.

If accepted, determine how the file is later served — with its stored, attacker-controlled Content-Type header, which would enable a browser to render/execute it as originally intended by the attacker despite the misleading extension.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes file-upload testing against a running build of the reviewed application.
Craft a file whose actual content is an XSS payload (or a web-shell script for a server-side-execution scenario) with a mismatched, innocuous-looking declared Content-Type/extension.
Upload the crafted file and confirm it's accepted despite the content/type mismatch.

Access the uploaded file via its resulting URL and confirm whether it's served in a way that triggers the embedded payload (executed as script, or served with a Content-Type causing the browser to render rather than download it).
Document the exact source location of the trust-in-client-supplied-type logic and the confirmed runtime exploitation.
Document exact reproduction steps with all commands, parameters, headers, and environmental conditions for reproducibility by any team member

SRC-003.prerequisites: Read access to the full application source code and its version-control history (not just the current HEAD, since a credential may have been removed from the latest commit but remain in history). Standard string-search and secret-scanning tools (grep/ripgrep, gitleaks, truffleHog).
SRC-003.whatItIs: The source code has a password, API key, or other credential typed directly into it, or into a configuration file that's checked into the code repository — instead of being loaded securely at runtime from an environment variable or a proper secrets service.
SRC-003.rootCause: Typing a credential straight into the code is the fastest way to get something working during development. Without an automated scan checking for this during code review, it's easy to miss — especially when the credential was added quickly to unblock one specific task, rather than through a careful, reviewed setup process.
SRC-003.impact: Anyone with read access to the source repository — every developer, anyone with access to a leaked/breached copy of the repo, or the general public if the repository is or ever becomes public — obtains the credential directly, and because it's embedded in code, it also persists in every historical commit, every fork, and every backup/mirror of the repository indefinitely, vastly widening the population with access relative to a runtime-only secret.
stepsToIdentify: Run an automated secret-scanning tool across the full repository, including its complete commit history, not just the current working tree.

Manually grep for common credential-indicating patterns (`password =`, `api_key =`, `secret =`, cloud-provider key formats) as a complement to automated scanning, which can miss non-standard variable naming.
For each candidate found, trace its usage to confirm it's a genuine, live credential rather than an obviously-fake placeholder/example value.

Where a credential was found removed from the current HEAD but present in history, confirm whether it was also rotated, since removal from the current commit alone doesn't invalidate a credential that remains readable in history.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes credential extraction and, where applicable, validation from the reviewed source code/repository.
Run secret-scanning across the full repository history and manually review flagged candidates.
For each confirmed candidate, validate its live status and scope of access using a minimal, read-only check appropriate to the credential type.
Document every discovered credential, its exact source location (including whether it's only in history versus also the current HEAD), and its validated scope of access.
Recommend immediate rotation for any confirmed live, exposed credential as an urgent finding, independent of the rest of the report.

SRC-004.prerequisites: Read access to the source code responsible for generating session tokens/identifiers. A running build of the application to collect a sample of generated tokens for statistical validation of the source-level finding.
SRC-004.whatItIs: Looking directly at the code that generates session tokens: it uses a source of randomness that isn't actually unpredictable enough for something this sensitive — an ordinary random function instead of a cryptographically secure one, or a token built mostly from predictable pieces like a timestamp or a simple counter.
SRC-004.rootCause: A session token needs to be just as unpredictable as an encryption key. But reaching for a standard, everyday random function (which is simpler, and fine for non-security uses) instead of deliberately choosing a cryptographically secure one is an easy mistake to make, especially if it's not obvious from the surrounding code that this particular value is actually security-critical.
SRC-004.impact: An attacker who can characterize the generator's algorithm and any predictable seed/input (straightforward for well-documented non-cryptographic PRNGs, whose internal state is often fully reconstructable from a handful of observed outputs) can predict other users' session tokens, enabling session hijacking without ever needing to steal a token via a separate vector like XSS or network interception.
stepsToIdentify: Locate the exact code path generating session tokens/identifiers and identify the specific randomness API used.

Confirm whether the API is a cryptographically secure generator (`SecureRandom`, `crypto.randomBytes`) or a standard, non-cryptographic one (`Math.random()`, `java.util.Random`, a weak hash of predictable input).
Where a CSPRNG is used, check how it's seeded, since a predictable seed can undermine an otherwise-correct algorithm choice.

Collect a sample of generated tokens from a running build (for test accounts) and statistically analyze them for patterns consistent with the weak generator identified in source, confirming the source-level finding is practically exploitable.

Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies

Extract or replicate the exact generation algorithm and seeding logic identified in source.

SRC-005.prerequisites: Read access to the authentication-logic source code. A running build of the application and an HTTP client (curl/Burp Suite) to confirm the identified logic flaw's runtime behavior.
SRC-005.whatItIs: Reading the actual login-checking code reveals a specific coding mistake that lets someone get in without a real, valid password — an 'if' condition written backwards or with a subtle bug, code that returns success before the password check has actually finished running, a comparison that can be tricked by a specially crafted input, or a 'remember me' or single-sign-on path that skips the real password check entirely under certain conditions.
SRC-005.rootCause: Login logic tends to accumulate multiple paths over time — regular password login, single sign-on, 'remember me,' API-key login — often added by different developers at different times. A subtle bug in any one of those paths can create a bypass. This is fundamentally a coding mistake in security-critical logic, and it's the kind of thing that's often only really catchable by carefully reading the exact code, not just testing the app from outside.
SRC-005.impact: An attacker who identifies and can trigger the specific flawed condition achieves full authentication bypass — logging in as any user, including an administrator, without any valid credential — which is among the most severe possible findings since it undermines the entire security model built on top of the assumption that authentication is a reliable gate.
stepsToIdentify: Read the complete authentication-logic code path line by line, tracing every conditional branch from request receipt to the final authenticated/rejected decision, for every supported authentication method (password, SSO, remember-me, API key).

Pay particular attention to negation operators, early-return statements, and comparison operators (especially loose/coercive equality in dynamically-typed languages) that could behave unexpectedly for a specific, crafted input.
For each suspicious construct identified, reason through what specific input would trigger the unintended code path, and note it as a hypothesis to validate at runtime.
Build and run the application, then attempt the crafted input against the identified code path to confirm whether the bypass is practically exploitable.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies

SRC-006.prerequisites: Read access to the session-management source code (session creation, regeneration, and invalidation logic). A running build of the application and an HTTP client (curl/Burp Suite) capable of manipulating and reusing session identifiers across requests.
SRC-006.whatItIs: The session-handling code fails to issue a brand-new session ID at a key moment — most commonly, right after someone successfully logs in. That means a session ID that existed before login (one an attacker might have set up in advance and tricked the victim into using, or simply observed) keeps working as the actual authenticated session once login completes.
SRC-006.rootCause: Preventing this kind of attack requires a deliberate step — explicitly generating a fresh session ID at the exact moment someone's access level changes, especially at login. That step is easy to miss if the session framework being used doesn't do it automatically, or if the session-handling code was custom-built without this specific protection in mind.
SRC-006.impact: An attacker who can cause a victim to use a session identifier the attacker knows in advance (via a URL parameter accepting a session ID, a predictable session-cookie-setting mechanism, or simply setting the cookie in a shared/kiosk browser context before the victim logs in) can then use that same, now-authenticated session identifier themselves after the victim logs in, hijacking the victim's authenticated session without ever needing to steal a credential or a post-login token.
stepsToIdentify: Locate the session-creation and login-handling code and trace whether a new session identifier is generated/issued specifically at the point of successful authentication, versus the pre-login session identifier simply being "upgraded" to an authenticated state in place.
Build and run the application, then capture the session identifier issued before login.

Complete a login using that same pre-established session identifier (not allowing the client to accept a new cookie if one is offered) and confirm whether the identifier remains valid and now represents the authenticated session.
Where regeneration is confirmed absent, also check for the same gap at other privilege-transition points (a password change, an MFA step-up) beyond just the initial login.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies

SRC-007.prerequisites: Read access to the application's role/privilege-management source code. A running build of the application and valid credentials for at least two accounts of different intended privilege levels to confirm the identified logic gap at runtime.
SRC-007.whatItIs: The code that assigns, checks, or upgrades a user's permission level has a flaw that lets someone end up with more access than intended — a function that defaults to giving admin-level access when some expected piece of information is missing, an admin-promotion feature with no check on who's allowed to use it, or a role that's read from something the client can modify (like a cookie or token) instead of being independently confirmed on the server every time.
SRC-007.rootCause: This kind of code is usually written and tested for the normal, expected case, without enough thought given to what happens when something unexpected or missing shows up — like defaulting to a high-privilege role instead of the lowest one when input is missing — or whether the function that actually grants elevated access has its own permission check guarding who can call it.
SRC-007.impact: A user can end up with (or grant themselves/another account) a higher privilege level than intended, ranging from a minor, unintended feature-access expansion to full administrative control of the application, depending on exactly which privilege-management flaw is present.
stepsToIdentify: Locate all code responsible for assigning or checking user roles/privileges, including account-creation defaults, role-elevation/promotion functions, and any place a role value is read from a client-supplied source (a JWT claim, a cookie, a hidden form field).

For a role-assignment default, trace what happens if the expected input determining the role is missing/null — does the code default to the least-privileged role, or does an unhandled case inadvertently resolve to something more permissive.
For a role-elevation/promotion function, confirm it has its own, independent authorization check restricting who can invoke it, separate from simply being an authenticated user.

For any role value sourced from client-modifiable data, confirm whether the server treats it as authoritative without re-deriving/re-validating it against the actual, stored account role on each request.

SRC-008.prerequisites: Read access to the application's request-handling/controller source code for a representative set of endpoints. A running build of the application and valid credentials for at least two accounts of differing privilege/ownership to confirm the identified gap at runtime.
SRC-008.whatItIs: A specific piece of code handling a sensitive action — returning data, changing a record, doing something admin-level — correctly checks that the caller is logged in, but never actually checks whether they're allowed to do this specific thing. Tracing through the code directly confirms there's no ownership or role check anywhere in that path at all.
SRC-008.rootCause: A permission check has to be deliberately added to every sensitive piece of code — it doesn't happen automatically. It's easy for one specific endpoint (especially one added later, or copied from a similar one without adjusting the checks, or one whose sensitivity the original developer didn't fully appreciate) to simply never get that check written in the first place — as opposed to having a check that's just flawed.
SRC-008.impact: Any authenticated (or in the most severe cases, even unauthenticated) caller can invoke the affected function and perform whatever sensitive action it exposes, entirely unconstrained by any ownership or role requirement — this is a complete absence of a control rather than a weakness in one, so impact is generally severe and directly proportional to the sensitivity of the specific unprotected function.
stepsToIdentify: For each endpoint/function handling a sensitive action, trace its complete execution path from request receipt to the action being performed, explicitly confirming whether an authorization check (ownership verification, role check) exists anywhere in that path.

Pay particular attention to newer endpoints, endpoints that appear structurally similar to another, properly-authorized endpoint (suggesting a copy-paste origin that may have dropped the check), and endpoints reached via an unusual or secondary code path (a batch-operation handler, an internal API called by another service).
For any function found with no authorization check at all, confirm this isn't compensated for by a check performed earlier in a shared middleware chain that the specific route might bypass.
Build and run the application, then confirm the finding at runtime by invoking the function using an account that should not be authorized for it.

SRC-018.rootCause: A weak or outdated algorithm was likely chosen back when the code was first written — maybe it seemed fine at the time, or it was just the first, familiar option available — and it was never revisited or upgraded since. Sometimes a library's own default setting quietly picks a weaker option than the developer realized, simply because they didn't explicitly specify a stronger one.
SRC-018.impact: Depending on the specific weak algorithm/mode, impact ranges from data patterns being visible in ciphertext (ECB mode, potentially revealing structural information about encrypted data), to full practical decryption/collision feasibility for genuinely broken algorithms (DES's small key space, RC4's known keystream biases, MD5/SHA-1's collision vulnerabilities for any application relying on collision-resistance specifically, such as a digital-signature scheme).

SRC-024.prerequisites: Read access to the application's error/exception-handling source code, particularly a global/top-level error handler. A running build of the application and an HTTP client to trigger a representative unhandled error condition and confirm the identified handling gap at runtime.
SRC-024.whatItIs: When something goes wrong, the application's error-handling code sends the raw error details straight back to the user — a full stack trace, an internal file path, a database error revealing table structure — instead of a generic, safe message. This is confirmed by finding the code that handles unexpected errors and checking exactly what detail it includes in the response sent to the user.
SRC-024.rootCause: A generic error handler that just returns whatever error it caught is a common, quick way to build things during development, since it's genuinely useful for debugging. It's easy for that same behavior to get left in place once the app goes live, either because nobody specifically went back to change it for production, or because the framework's own default behavior is verbose unless someone explicitly configures it not to be.
SRC-024.impact: Verbose error responses leak internal implementation detail useful for further attack planning — a stack trace revealing the exact framework/library versions in use (aiding a targeted CVE search), internal file paths revealing server directory structure, or a database error message revealing table/column names that narrow down a SQL-injection attempt — and in some cases, the leaked detail itself may include genuinely sensitive data (a connection string embedded in an exception message).

SRC-028.impact: An attacker able to intercept or redirect the download (a network MITM position, a compromised distribution server/CDN, or a DNS-based redirection) can deliver an arbitrary, malicious artifact that the application then executes/loads with its own trust and privilege level, resulting in full compromise.

SRC-031.whatItIs: Code that reads or writes a file based on a filename or path the caller supplies builds the final file location by directly gluing that value onto a base folder path, without checking for or stripping out sequences like '../' that could let someone escape outside the intended folder. SRC-031.impact: An attacker can read (or, for a write operation, overwrite) arbitrary files on the file system that the application process has permission to access, potentially exposing sensitive configuration files, source code, or credentials, or in a write scenario, overwriting a critical application file to achieve further compromise.

Build and run the application, then submit a traversal-sequence-crafted value (`../../../../etc/passwd` or an OS-appropriate equivalent) to the identified parameter.
Confirm whether the response reflects content from outside the intended base directory, proving the traversal succeeded.
For a write-capable file-access function, similarly test whether a traversal sequence can direct a write operation outside the intended directory.

SRC-032.prerequisites: Read access to logging-call source code across representative endpoints. A running build of the application and access to its log output (or log-aggregation system, with client authorization) to confirm the identified logging gap at runtime.
SRC-032.whatItIs: Logging statements in the code capture sensitive data — a password from a request, an auth token, a card number, or other personal information — and write it directly into the logs. This is confirmed by finding the logging call and seeing that what gets logged includes those sensitive fields instead of a cleaned-up, filtered version.
SRC-032.rootCause: Logging an entire request or response is a common, convenient way to get maximum detail for debugging — and it's easy to forget that what's being logged might include fields that really shouldn't end up in a log file at all, especially if that logging line was added quickly during development or while troubleshooting an issue, and never revisited before going live.
SRC-032.impact: Anyone with access to the log output or log-aggregation system — which is frequently a broader population than those authorized to see the underlying sensitive data directly (a wider engineering/support team, a third-party log-aggregation vendor) — can read the logged sensitive data, and log retention periods often exceed how long the same data would be retained in its primary, intended storage location.

For each candidate, confirm whether the logged content includes genuinely sensitive fields (password, token, card number, PII) rather than a filtered/redacted subset.
Build and run the application, populate representative sensitive test data through normal use, and inspect the actual log output for the presence of that data in plaintext.
Check whether a third-party log-aggregation service is used, which would extend the population with access beyond the organization's own personnel.

Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies

SRC-033.prerequisites: Read access to source code that fetches a URL server-side based on caller-supplied input (a webhook-registration handler, a file-import-by-URL feature, a link-preview generator). A running build of the application and a listener you control (Burp Collaborator or netcat) to confirm the identified SSRF at runtime.
SRC-033.whatItIs: A function that makes a server-side request to a web address built from caller-supplied input does so with no restriction on where that address is allowed to point. This is confirmed by finding the code that makes the outbound request and tracing its target address back to something the caller can actually influence.
SRC-033.rootCause: This URL-fetching code was built to support a real, useful feature without adding any restriction on where it's allowed to send requests — treating the caller-supplied address as trustworthy, rather than as untrusted data that could point the server's own network requests anywhere it's able to reach.
SRC-033.impact: An attacker can cause the server to make arbitrary requests to internal-only network resources or a cloud provider's instance-metadata service, using the server's own network position and trust to reach targets the attacker couldn't otherwise access directly.
stepsToIdentify: Locate every function performing a server-side HTTP(S) request based on caller-supplied input and confirm whether any destination-restriction logic (an allowlist, an internal-IP block) exists before the request is made.
Build and run the application, then submit a request with the target-URL parameter pointing at a listener you control to confirm the server fetches it.
Submit the same request with the target-URL parameter pointing at an internal/link-local address and observe the response for reflected content.
Test whether alternate URL schemes (`file://`, `gopher://`) are also accepted, indicating a broader SSRF primitive.
Review target configuration files and deployment manifests — check for hardcoded credentials, overly permissive ACLs, debug mode in production, default credentials
Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies

Submit a test request with the target-URL parameter pointing at a Collaborator/controlled listener to confirm out-of-band request delivery.

SRC-034.prerequisites: Read access to the application's dependency manifest (package.json/requirements.txt/pom.xml and their corresponding lock files). A software-composition-analysis (SCA) tool (npm audit, OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk, or an equivalent) to scan the manifest for known vulnerabilities.
SRC-034.whatItIs: The application depends on a third-party library at a version with one or more known, publicly documented security bugs. This is found by directly scanning the list of dependencies against a database of known vulnerabilities, rather than waiting to see an actual attack happen.
SRC-034.rootCause: Dependencies typically get locked to a specific version when they're first added, and only get updated when a new feature is needed or there's a scheduled window to do the testing an update requires. Without a regular, deliberate process to check dependencies against new vulnerability disclosures, a locked-in version just quietly builds up known, unpatched security bugs over time.
SRC-034.impact: Any known vulnerability in the outdated dependency becomes directly exploitable against the application if the vulnerable code path is reachable from the application's actual usage of that library — ranging from a low-risk, unused code path to a directly exploitable remote-code-execution or authentication-bypass vulnerability depending on the specific CVE.

Review the resulting CVE findings, prioritizing Critical/High severity issues with a known public exploit.
For each Critical/High finding, review the application's actual usage of the affected library/function to assess whether the vulnerable code path is genuinely reachable.
Cross-reference the dependency's pinned version against its current, actively-maintained release to quantify how far behind the integration has drifted.

SRC-035.prerequisites: Read access to source code that parses XML input (an API endpoint accepting XML, a file-import feature processing an uploaded XML/SVG/DOCX-family document). A running build of the application and an HTTP client to confirm the identified XXE gap at runtime.
SRC-035.whatItIs: The application processes XML data supplied by a caller using a parser that hasn't turned off a feature called external entity resolution. This is confirmed directly by finding the XML-parsing code and checking whether the specific settings that disable this risky feature are actually turned on — or left at their default, permissive state.
SRC-035.rootCause: Most XML parsing tools have historically allowed this feature by default, for compatibility with the XML standard. Unless the application specifically turns it off when setting up the parser, any XML it processes — including XML from an untrusted source — can reference external content that the parser will go fetch, whether that's reading a local file or making an outbound network request the attacker directed.
SRC-035.impact: An attacker can craft XML input containing a malicious external entity definition that, when parsed, reads and discloses local file contents (a classic XXE file-read via an entity referencing `file:///etc/passwd` or an application configuration file), or triggers a server-side-request-forgery-style outbound request (referencing an internal or cloud-metadata URL), or in some parser/library configurations, causes a denial-of-service via an entity-expansion ("billion laughs") attack.

Where the parser configuration is default/unconfigured for these settings, treat this as a strong indicator of vulnerability pending runtime confirmation.
Build and run the application, then submit a crafted XML payload containing an external entity referencing a benign, verifiable local file or an out-of-band listener.
Confirm whether the response reflects the referenced file's content, or whether an out-of-band request is received, proving the entity was resolved.

Test with authenticated and unauthenticated access levels to identify authorization boundary discrepancies
